body:
## Problem

`packaging>=24.0` is declared as a runtime dependency but is never imported by
any module in the package. It ships to every end user of `ghaw-auditor`.

## Evidence

Ecosystem: Python (uv). `packaging@25.0`.

1. **Manifest** — `pyproject.toml:19`, `[project].dependencies` (production section):
   `"packaging>=24.0",`
2. **Lockfile** — `uv.lock:333` `name = "packaging"` / `version = "25.0"`;
   declared as a direct dependency of the root package at `uv.lock:170` and
   recorded in `[package.metadata].requires-dist` at `uv.lock:194`.
   It is *also* pulled in transitively at `uv.lock:464` (pytest's dependency),
   so nothing would fail to resolve if the direct declaration were dropped.
3. **Usage scan** — exhaustive negative. Full import-form coverage over the
   tracked tree:
   - `grep -rhoE '^\s*(from|import)\s+[a-zA-Z0-9_.]+' ghaw_auditor/ tests/`
     enumerates every import in the project; `packaging` appears in neither the
     source nor the test import set.
   - No `importlib`, `__import__`, `entry_points`, or `pkg_resources` anywhere
     (`grep -rn 'importlib\|__import__\|entry_points\|pkg_resources'` → no hits),
     so there is no dynamic-import escape hatch.
   - `git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -nE 'packaging'` returns exactly three
     kinds of hit and no others: the `pyproject.toml:19` declaration, and
     `uv.lock` lines 170/194/333/336/338/464. Zero hits in `ghaw_auditor/`,
     `tests/`, `Makefile`, `.github/`, or any config file.
   - Import name equals package name (`packaging`), so no name-mapping gap.

## Impact

Every install of `ghaw-auditor` resolves and downloads a package the code never
calls. It widens the production dependency graph — and therefore the CVE and
supply-chain surface — for zero functionality.

The likelier reading is a latent bug rather than dead weight: `resolver.py` and
`differ.py` compare action version tags, and `packaging` is the obvious library
for that. It was declared and never wired up, which means version comparison is
being done some other way (string comparison) and may be wrong on cases like
`v10` vs `v9`.

## Fix

Confirm which of the two is true before acting:

- If version comparison is genuinely not needed, remove the declaration:
  ```bash
  uv remove packaging
  ```
  (leaves `packaging` present as a pytest transitive; nothing breaks)
- If `resolver.py`/`differ.py` are string-comparing versions, that is a
  correctness bug and `packaging.version.Version` is the fix — wire it up
  rather than removing the dependency.

Removal is behavior-affecting and requires explicit per-dependency approval.

## Resolution
Removed via 'uv remove packaging'. CORRECTION to this finding's Impact section: the hypothesis that resolver.py/differ.py were string-comparing versions is WRONG. Investigation found no version-comparison logic anywhere - resolver.py resolves a ref to a SHA via the GitHub API (resolver.py:100-117) and never parses or orders versions; ActionRef.ref (models.py:28) is an opaque string. packaging was declared for a feature never built, so removal is unambiguously correct. Verified: no 'packaging' in pyproject.toml; still present in uv.lock as a pytest transitive as predicted. 211 tests pass, mypy 2.3.0 clean. Separate real bug found during the investigation and routed to /nitpicker review: differ.py:174-176 marks every pre-existing action 'unchanged' regardless of ref/SHA change.
title: Unused production dependency: packaging

body:
## Problem

`vcrpy>=6.0.0` is declared in the `dev` extra to record and replay HTTP
interactions, but no test uses it. The HTTP tests mock by hand instead.

## Evidence

Ecosystem: Python (uv). `vcrpy@8.2.1`.

1. **Manifest** — `pyproject.toml:27`, `[project.optional-dependencies].dev`:
   `"vcrpy>=6.0.0",`
2. **Lockfile** — `uv.lock:749` `name = "vcrpy"` / `version = "8.2.1"`; listed
   as a dev-extra dependency of the root package at `uv.lock:186` and in
   `requires-dist` at `uv.lock:205`. It drags in two transitives of its own,
   `pyyaml` (`uv.lock:753`) and `wrapt` (`uv.lock:754`).
3. **Usage scan** — exhaustive negative.
   - Import name is `vcr`, not `vcrpy` (name mapping applied).
     `git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -niE '\bvcr'` returns only
     `pyproject.toml:27` and the `uv.lock` lines above — zero hits in `tests/`.
   - The test import set contains `pytest`, `httpx`, `json`, `logging`,
     `unittest.mock`, `pathlib`, `datetime`, `tenacity`, `typer.testing` and
     first-party `ghaw_auditor.*` — no `vcr`.
   - No cassette directory exists (`tests/` holds only `fixtures/` YAML and
     `golden/` JSON+MD).
   - No `importlib`/`__import__` dynamic loading anywhere in the tree.
   - Not a pytest plugin auto-loaded via config: `[tool.pytest.ini_options]`
     (`pyproject.toml:58-62`) declares only `testpaths`, `python_files`,
     `python_functions`, `addopts` — no `plugins` entry.

## Impact

Dev-only, so it never reaches production installs. It costs every contributor
and every CI run the download and install of vcrpy plus `pyyaml` and `wrapt`.
`pyyaml` is the notable one: it is the *only* reason PyYAML is in the lock at
all, which in turn is what makes the `types-PyYAML` stub declaration look
justified when it is not.

## Fix

```bash
uv remove --optional dev vcrpy
```
This also drops `pyyaml` and `wrapt` from the lock. Removal requires explicit
per-dependency approval.

If HTTP-recording tests are actually wanted, the fix is the opposite direction:
write them. `tests/test_github_client.py` currently hand-mocks `httpx`.

## Resolution
Removed via 'uv remove --optional dev vcrpy'. Transitives pyyaml and wrapt dropped from uv.lock with it. Re-scan: 'grep -niE \bvcr' over all tracked files returns zero hits. 211 tests pass, 100% coverage unchanged.
title: Unused dev dependency: vcrpy

body:
## Problem

`types-PyYAML` is declared in the `dev` extra. It provides type stubs for
**PyYAML** (import name `yaml`). This project parses YAML with **ruamel.yaml**
and never imports `yaml`, so the stubs type a library that is not used.

## Evidence

Ecosystem: Python (uv). `types-PyYAML@6.0.12.20250915`.

1. **Manifest** — `pyproject.toml:30`, `[project.optional-dependencies].dev`:
   `"types-PyYAML",` — note it also carries **no version specifier**, the only
   declaration in either section without one.
2. **Lockfile** — `uv.lock:185` (dev extra of the root package) and
   `requires-dist` at `uv.lock:204`, where it is the only entry with no
   `specifier` field. The stubbed package `pyyaml@6.0.3` is at `uv.lock:488`,
   and it is present **only** as a transitive of `vcrpy` (`uv.lock:753`) —
   PyYAML is declared nowhere in `pyproject.toml`.
3. **Usage scan** — exhaustive negative.
   - `git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -nE '^\s*(import yaml|from yaml)'`
     → no hits. Nothing in the tree imports PyYAML's `yaml` module.
   - The source import set contains `from ruamel.yaml` (the actual YAML
     library, `pyproject.toml:16`), never bare `yaml`.
   - Stub packages are consumed by type checkers via the import graph only;
     with no `import yaml` there is no import for mypy to resolve against them.
   - No `[[tool.mypy.overrides]]` or `mypy_path` entry references the stubs
     (`[tool.mypy]` at `pyproject.toml:51-56` sets only `python_version`,
     `strict`, `warn_return_any`, `warn_unused_configs`, `disallow_untyped_defs`).

## Impact

Dev-only. Two compounding effects:

1. The stubs are inert — removing them cannot change any mypy result, because
   mypy never resolves a `yaml` import.
2. It is misleading. It reads as "our YAML usage is typed", while the actual
   YAML library in use, `ruamel.yaml`, ships no inline types and has its own
   separate stub distribution. If `strict = true` is genuinely passing today,
   it is not because of this package.

The missing version specifier is a second, smaller problem: stub packages are
date-versioned and track upstream's API, so an unpinned stub can change what
type-checks between two runs with no manifest change.

## Fix

```bash
uv remove --optional dev types-PyYAML
```
Removal requires explicit per-dependency approval.

If typed YAML handling is the actual goal, the correct package for this
codebase is `types-ruamel.yaml`, not `types-PyYAML` — and it should carry a
version specifier like every other declaration.

## Resolution
Removed via 'uv remove --optional dev types-PyYAML'. Re-scan: no types-pyyaml in any tracked file; pyyaml also gone from uv.lock (it was only a vcrpy transitive). The finding's central claim is now empirically confirmed: mypy 2.3.0 reports 'Success: no issues found in 29 source files' with the stubs absent, so they were provably inert.
title: Unused dev dependency: types-PyYAML stubs a library the project never imports

body:
## Problem

`ruff>=0.3.0` is declared in the `dev` extra, but every place that actually runs
ruff invokes it through `uvx`, which resolves an **isolated** tool install and
ignores the project environment. The declared constraint therefore never governs
which ruff runs — including in CI.

## Evidence

Ecosystem: Python (uv). `ruff@0.13.2` locked; `0.16.2` current on PyPI.

1. **Manifest** — `pyproject.toml:29`, `[project.optional-dependencies].dev`:
   `"ruff>=0.3.0",`
2. **Lockfile** — `uv.lock:612` `name = "ruff"` / `version = "0.13.2"`; dev
   extra of the root package at `uv.lock:184`, `requires-dist` at `uv.lock:201`.
   So `uv sync --extra dev` really does install ruff 0.13.2 into `.venv`.
3. **Usage scan** — every ruff invocation in the tree, via
   `git ls-files -z | xargs -0 grep -nE 'ruff'`:
   - `.github/workflows/pr.yml:24` — `run: uvx ruff check .`
   - `Makefile:21` — `uvx ruff check .`
   - `Makefile:24` — `uvx ruff format .`
   - `CONTRIBUTING.md:24-25`, `README.md:314,317,473-474` — all `uvx ruff`
   - `.pre-commit-config.yaml:47-54` — `astral-sh/ruff-pre-commit` at its own
     `rev: v0.16.2`, a third independent version
   There is **no** `uv run ruff` anywhere. `[tool.ruff]` at `pyproject.toml:40-49`
   configures whichever binary runs; it is not a reference to the declared
   dependency.

## Impact

Three different ruff versions are in play for one project: `0.13.2` in the lock,
whatever `uvx` resolves as latest at run time (`0.16.2` today), and `v0.16.2`
pinned in pre-commit.

The CI consequence is the concrete one. `.github/workflows/pr.yml:24` runs
`uvx ruff check .`, which fetches the newest ruff on every run. A PR that passes
lint today can fail tomorrow with no change to the repo, because ruff shipped a
new rule overnight — a green branch goes red on re-run. That is exactly the
non-reproducibility the lockfile exists to prevent, and the lock is being
bypassed.

Note `mypy` has the same split but lands the other way: CI uses `uv run mypy .`
(`pr.yml:27`, honours the lock) while `Makefile:27` and the docs use `uvx mypy .`
(does not). So local and CI type-checking do not agree either.

## Fix

Make the declared dependency the one that runs. In `.github/workflows/pr.yml:24`
and `Makefile:21,24`:

```diff
-	uvx ruff check .
+	uv run ruff check .
-	uvx ruff format .
+	uv run ruff format .
```
and in `Makefile:27` for consistency with CI:
```diff
-	uvx mypy .
+	uv run mypy .
```
Then update `CONTRIBUTING.md:24-25,28` and `README.md:314,317,320,473-475` to
match. Keep `ruff` in the dev extra — after this change it is genuinely used,
and the lock pins it.

Keep `.pre-commit-config.yaml`'s ruff `rev` in sync with the locked version so
all three agree.

The alternative — dropping `ruff` from the dev extra and accepting `uvx` — is
worse: it makes CI lint permanently unpinned by design.

## Resolution
Switched every dev-tool invocation from uvx to uv run so the lockfile governs: .github/workflows/pr.yml:24, Makefile:21,24,27, CONTRIBUTING.md:24,25,28, README.md:314,317,320,473,474,475. CI lint is now reproducible - it runs locked ruff 0.16.2 instead of whatever uvx fetches. pre-commit ruff rev (v0.16.2) now matches the locked version. Makefile .PHONY also corrected to include the typecheck target it defines. Deliberately left alone: 'uvx ghaw-auditor' in README, which is the tool's own documented install-free usage, not dev tooling.
title: Declared ruff dev dependency never binds: every invocation uses uvx, so lint runs unpinned

body:
## Problem

Both `scan` and `validate` accept a `--policy-file` path, check that it exists,
and then discard it. A hardcoded default `Policy()` is used instead. The user
believes their policy is being enforced; it is not.

## Evidence

`cli.py:126-129` (scan):
```python
policy = None
if policy_file and policy_file.exists():
    # TODO: Load policy from YAML file
    policy = Policy()
```
`cli.py:240-243` (validate):
```python
policy = Policy()
if policy_file and policy_file.exists():
    # TODO: Parse YAML policy file here
    pass
```
The file is opened for an `.exists()` check and never read. `Policy()` is the
default from `models.py:192-201`: `min_permissions=True`,
`require_pinned_actions=True`, `forbid_branch_refs=False`,
`allowed_actions=[]`, `denied_actions=[]`, `require_concurrency_on_pr=False`.

README documents this flag as working in seven places — `README.md:40,133,237,240,334`
plus a full `policy.yml` schema example at `README.md:207`. `CHANGELOG.md`
lists "Policy validation with enforcement" as a shipped 1.0.0 feature.

Failing scenario: a user writes
```yaml
denied_actions: ["evil-org/*"]
forbid_branch_refs: true
```
and runs `ghaw-auditor validate --policy policy.yml --enforce` in CI.
`denied_actions` stays `[]` and `forbid_branch_refs` stays `False`, so a
workflow using `evil-org/backdoor@main` produces **zero** violations from those
rules and CI passes green. The user has a policy gate that enforces nothing
they wrote.

Tests do not catch it: `test_cli.py:111-127,557-580` write a real `policy.yml`
containing `require_pinned_actions: true`, pass `--policy-file`, and assert only
that the command exits cleanly. They would pass identically if the flag were
deleted.

## Impact

This is the central promised feature of a security-auditing tool, and it fails
open and silently. A team can adopt this in CI, write a strict policy, see a
green build, and conclude their workflows are compliant when no rule they
authored was ever evaluated. Silent policy bypass is worse than no policy —
it manufactures false assurance.

## Fix

Load the file into the `Policy` model. `ruamel.yaml` is already a dependency
and `Policy` is already a pydantic model, so this is a parse plus validate:

```python
def _load_policy(policy_file: Path | None) -> Policy | None:
    if policy_file is None:
        return None
    if not policy_file.exists():
        raise typer.BadParameter(f"Policy file not found: {policy_file}")
    yaml = YAML(typ="safe")
    with open(policy_file, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        data = yaml.load(fh) or {}
    return Policy.model_validate(data)
```
Call it from both commands. A missing `--policy` path must be a hard error, not
a silent fallback to defaults — the current `and policy_file.exists()` guard
turns a typo in the path into a silent downgrade to the default policy.

## Resolution
Implemented _load_policy (cli.py) using ruamel.yaml + Policy.model_validate; wired into both scan and validate. Missing path, invalid YAML, non-mapping and schema failures are now typer.BadParameter, not a silent fallback to defaults. Verified end-to-end: a policy with denied_actions/forbid_branch_refs now produces violations, and one setting require_pinned_actions:false genuinely suppresses them. 5 new CLI tests.
title: --policy FILE is silently ignored; the default policy is enforced instead

body:
## Problem

GitHub Actions allows `permissions: read-all` and `permissions: write-all` as
bare strings. The parser matches the string form, throws the value away, and
returns a default `Permissions()` with every field `None` — byte-identical to a
workflow that declares no permissions at all.

## Evidence

`parser.py:107-116`:
```python
def _parse_permissions(self, perms: Any) -> Permissions | None:
    if perms is None:
        return None
    if isinstance(perms, str):
        # Global read-all or write-all
        return Permissions()  # <-- value discarded
```
`Permissions` (`models.py:83-97`) has twelve fields, all defaulting to `None`.

Reproduced against a real workflow declaring `permissions: write-all`:
```
2) permissions: write-all  ->  parsed as: actions=None checks=None contents=None
   deployments=None id_token=None issues=None packages=None pages=None
   pull_requests=None repository_projects=None security_events=None statuses=None
   indistinguishable from absent? True
```

Downstream consequences, all silent:
- `analyzer._analyze_permissions` (`analyzer.py:44-51`) counts
  `sum(1 for w in workflows.values() if w.permissions)`. A `Permissions()`
  instance is truthy, so `write-all` is counted as "has permissions" —
  scored the same as a tightly scoped `contents: read`.
- `renderer._write_job_details` (`renderer.py:126-132`) filters
  `{k: v for k, v in ... if v is not None}`, gets an empty dict, and prints
  no Permissions block at all. The report for a `write-all` job is visually
  identical to one with no permissions.

The existing test locks the bug in: `test_parser.py:263-265` calls
`_parse_permissions("read-all")` and asserts only that an object comes back,
never that the level was captured.

## Impact

`permissions: write-all` grants the job token write access to every scope —
contents, packages, deployments, actions. It is the single most dangerous
permission declaration in GitHub Actions, and this tool renders it invisible in
both the analysis counts and the human-readable report. An auditor that cannot
see the worst case is worse than no auditor, because the clean report is taken
as evidence of safety.

## Fix

Represent the string forms explicitly by expanding them across all scopes:

```python
if isinstance(perms, str):
    if perms == "write-all":
        return Permissions(**dict.fromkeys(Permissions.model_fields, PermissionLevel.WRITE))
    if perms == "read-all":
        return Permissions(**dict.fromkeys(Permissions.model_fields, PermissionLevel.READ))
    if perms == "none":
        return Permissions(**dict.fromkeys(Permissions.model_fields, PermissionLevel.NONE))
    logger.warning(f"Unrecognized permissions value: {perms!r}")
    return None
```
Expanding rather than adding a flag keeps every downstream consumer
(analyzer, renderer, differ, policy) working unchanged and correct.
Add a test asserting `contents is PermissionLevel.WRITE` for `write-all`.

## Resolution
_parse_permissions now expands write-all/read-all/none across every scope via dict.fromkeys(Permissions.model_fields, level); unknown strings log a warning and return None. Re-ran the original repro: 'indistinguishable from absent?' flipped True -> False. End-to-end, write-all now surfaces as an ERROR violation. 3 new parser tests.
title: permissions: write-all is parsed as empty permissions, erasing the most dangerous setting

body:
## Problem

Every policy check filters on `action.type == ActionType.GITHUB`. Reusable
workflow calls are parsed as `ActionType.REUSABLE_WORKFLOW`, so an unpinned or
branch-pinned reusable workflow passes all policy rules silently.

## Evidence

`policy.py:64` (`_check_pinned_actions`):
```python
if action.type == ActionType.GITHUB and action.ref and not re.match(r"^[a-f0-9]{40}$", action.ref):
```
`policy.py:87` (`_check_branch_refs`) and `policy.py:109`
(`_check_action_allowlist`) apply the identical `== ActionType.GITHUB` filter.

`parser._parse_reusable_workflow_ref` (`parser.py:239-268`) always constructs
`ActionRef(type=ActionType.REUSABLE_WORKFLOW, ...)`, so the two sets never
intersect.

Reproduced with `require_pinned_actions=True` **and** `forbid_branch_refs=True`
against a workflow containing:
```yaml
  call:
    uses: some-org/some-repo/.github/workflows/build.yml@main
```
Result:
```
4) violations reported: 2
   - require_pinned_actions | Action actions/checkout is not pinned to SHA: v4
   - require_pinned_actions | Action actions/checkout is not pinned to SHA: v4
```
The reusable workflow on `@main` produces zero violations from either rule,
while the ordinary action is reported twice (tracked separately).

No test covers it: `grep -n 'REUSABLE\|reusable' tests/test_policy.py` returns
nothing.

## Impact

A called reusable workflow executes arbitrary steps in the caller's repository
context, with the caller's secrets when `secrets: inherit` is used. Pinning it
to a mutable branch is exactly the supply-chain exposure
`require_pinned_actions` and `forbid_branch_refs` exist to prevent — an upstream
force-push to `main` silently changes what runs. This is the highest-value
target in the whole reference graph, and it is the one the policy engine cannot
see. `denied_actions` and `allowed_actions` are bypassed the same way.

## Fix

Introduce the set of remotely-referenced types once and use it in all three
checks:

```python
_REMOTE_TYPES = (ActionType.GITHUB, ActionType.REUSABLE_WORKFLOW)
...
if action.type in _REMOTE_TYPES and action.ref and not _SHA_RE.match(action.ref):
```
`ActionRef.owner`/`.repo` are already populated for reusable workflows
(`parser.py:258-265`), so the existing message formatting needs no change.
Add policy tests covering a reusable workflow on `@main`, on `@v1`, and on a
full SHA.

## Resolution
Introduced REMOTE_ACTION_TYPES = (GITHUB, REUSABLE_WORKFLOW) and applied it in all three checks. The repro workflow's reusable call on @main now yields both require_pinned_actions and forbid_branch_refs violations where it previously yielded none. 3 new policy tests incl. a SHA-pinned reusable workflow staying clean.
title: Reusable workflows are exempt from require_pinned_actions and forbid_branch_refs

body:
## Problem

All three policy checks build their candidate list by concatenating
`workflow.actions_used` with each job's `actions_used`. But the parser already
populated `workflow.actions_used` as the union of all job actions, so every
action is examined twice and every violation is emitted twice.

## Evidence

`parser.py:76-80` builds the workflow-level list from the jobs:
```python
for job_name, job_data in jobs_data.items():
    job_meta = self._parse_job(job_name, job_data, path, content)
    jobs[job_name] = job_meta
    secrets_used.update(job_meta.secrets_used)
    actions_used.extend(job_meta.actions_used)  # <-- workflow list = union of job lists
```
`policy.py:58-60`, repeated verbatim at `81-83` and `104-106`:
```python
all_actions = workflow.actions_used[:]
for job in workflow.jobs.values():
    all_actions.extend(job.actions_used)  # <-- adds the same refs again
```

Reproduced on a workflow with exactly one `actions/checkout@v4` step:
```
3) workflow.actions_used   = ['actions/checkout@v4', 'some-org/.../build.yml@main']
   job[build].actions_used = ['actions/checkout@v4']
   job[call].actions_used  = ['some-org/.../build.yml@main']

4) violations reported: 2
   - require_pinned_actions | Action actions/checkout is not pinned to SHA: v4
   - require_pinned_actions | Action actions/checkout is not pinned to SHA: v4
```
One unpinned action, two identical violations.

The test suite cannot detect this: every count assertion in `test_policy.py`
(lines 51, 125, 166, 207, 226) is `len(violations) > 0`, never an exact number.
Lines 85 and 246 assert `== 0`. There is no test that would change behaviour if
the duplication were removed.

## Impact

- `console.print(f"Found {len(result.violations)} policy violations")`
  (`cli.py:150`) reports double the true count.
- `_enforce_policy` (`cli.py:88-93`) reports `len(error_violations)` — doubled.
- `violations.json` and the Markdown report list every violation twice
  (`renderer.py:236-246`), so a report with 40 real issues shows 80 entries.
- Users triaging a report cannot tell duplication from two genuinely distinct
  occurrences of the same action in different jobs — which is a real case the
  tool should distinguish.

## Fix

`workflow.actions_used` is already the complete set. Drop the job loop in all
three checks:

```python
for action in workflow.actions_used:
    ...
```
If per-job attribution is wanted in the violation message (a genuine
improvement), iterate jobs *only* and drop the workflow-level list instead —
but never both. Then tighten the tests to assert exact counts so a regression
is caught.

## Resolution
Dropped the redundant per-job loop in all three checks; workflow.actions_used is already the union. Verified: one unpinned action now yields exactly 1 violation, was 2. test_policy.py rewritten from 'len(violations) > 0' to exact counts so a regression is caught.
title: Every policy violation is reported twice: workflow.actions_used already contains all job actions

body:
## Problem

`scan` wraps its whole body in `except Exception`. `typer.Exit` subclasses
`RuntimeError`, hence `Exception`, so every deliberate exit raised inside the
`try` is caught by the generic handler and re-raised as `Exit(2)`.

## Evidence

Verified interactively:
```
1) typer.Exit MRO: ['Exit', 'RuntimeError', 'Exception', 'BaseException', 'object']
   caught by 'except Exception'? True
```
`cli.py:171-173`:
```python
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"Scan failed: {e}")
        raise typer.Exit(2) from None
```
Two deliberate exits are inside that `try`:
- `cli.py:121-123` — repository not found, raises `typer.Exit(1)`
- `cli.py:168-169` -> `_enforce_policy` (`cli.py:88-93`) — policy enforcement
  failure, raises `typer.Exit(1)`

Both are caught at line 171 and converted to `Exit(2)`. The `from None` also
suppresses the chained context, so the original intent is unrecoverable.

Failing scenario: CI runs `ghaw-auditor scan --enforce`. A policy violation
occurs. The user's pipeline distinguishes exit 1 (policy failed — post a review
comment) from exit 2 (tool crashed — page the on-call). It receives 2, and a
routine policy violation is escalated as a tool outage. The logs reinforce the
misdiagnosis: `logger.exception("Scan failed: 1")` prints a full traceback for
what was a clean, intentional exit.

`README.md` documents `--enforce` as "exit non-zero on violations", and
`cli.py:105` help text says the same, so the distinction is part of the
published contract.

## Impact

Exit codes are the entire machine-readable interface of a CLI gate. Collapsing
"policy violated" into "tool crashed" makes `--enforce` unusable for any
pipeline that branches on the code, and the spurious traceback sends users
debugging a failure that never happened.

## Fix

Let control-flow exceptions through before the generic handler:

```python
    except typer.Exit:
        raise
    except Exception as e:
        logger.exception(f"Scan failed: {e}")
        raise typer.Exit(2) from None
```
`typer.Abort` deserves the same passthrough. Add a test asserting
`result.exit_code == 1` for an enforced violation, which the current suite
never checks.

## Resolution
Added 'except typer.Exit: raise' and 'except typer.BadParameter: raise' ahead of the generic handler. Verified all five exit-code contracts: --enforce 1 (was 2), missing repo 1 (was 2), missing baseline 1 (was 0), clean 0, crash 2. Success banner also moved after _enforce_policy.
title: Blanket except Exception swallows typer.Exit, so --enforce failures exit 2 instead of 1

body:
## Problem

`Differ.diff_actions` detects added and removed action keys but never compares
two actions that exist in both baseline and current. It hardcodes
`status="unchanged"` with an empty change list.

## Evidence

`differ.py:174-176`:
```python
            elif baseline_action and current_action:
                # Compare (for now, just mark as unchanged)
                diffs.append(ActionDiff(key=key, status="unchanged", changes=[]))
```
`ActionDiff.status` (`models.py:230-235`) documents `modified` as a valid value;
nothing ever produces it. `_compare_workflows` (`differ.py:105-156`) does the
real field-by-field work for workflows — the action equivalent was never
written.

Failing scenario, and it is the tool's headline use case: run
`ghaw-auditor scan --write-baseline`, bump `actions/checkout` from a v4 SHA to a
v5 SHA, then run `ghaw-auditor scan --diff --baseline .audit/baseline`. The
report says the action is unchanged.

Note the key is `canonical_key()` (`models.py:33-41`), which for a GitHub action
is `owner/repo@resolved_sha or ref`. So a version bump changes the *key*, and
the diff reports it as one `removed` plus one `added` rather than a `modified`
with old/new — losing the fact that they are the same action. Meanwhile a
manifest whose content changed under a *stable* key (a mutable tag such as `v4`
repointed upstream, or a local action edited in place) reports `unchanged`
outright, even though `inputs`, `outputs`, `runs`, `is_docker` etc. all differ.
That mutable-tag case is precisely the supply-chain drift a baseline diff exists
to catch.

The test suite asserts the stub rather than the behaviour:
`test_differ.py:302-313` (`test_diff_actions_unchanged`) passes *the same object*
as both baseline and current and asserts `status == "unchanged"`. No test ever
passes two *different* manifests under one key, so the missing comparison is
invisible.

## Impact

`--diff` against a baseline is one of three documented commands
(`README.md:147-150`) and is listed in `CHANGELOG.md` as a shipped 1.0.0
feature. For the case that matters most — an action's manifest changing while
its reference stays the same — it reports "nothing changed". A reviewer relying
on the diff to approve a workflow change is told there is nothing to review.

## Fix

Implement the comparison the same way workflows already do it:

```python
def _compare_actions(self, old: ActionManifest, new: ActionManifest) -> list[DiffEntry]:
    changes: list[DiffEntry] = []
    for field in ("name", "description", "author", "runs", "is_composite", "is_docker", "is_javascript"):
        o, n = getattr(old, field), getattr(new, field)
        if o != n:
            changes.append(DiffEntry(field=field, old_value=o, new_value=n, change_type="modified"))
    for field in ("inputs", "outputs"):
        o = {k: v.model_dump() for k, v in getattr(old, field).items()}
        n = {k: v.model_dump() for k, v in getattr(new, field).items()}
        if o != n:
            changes.append(DiffEntry(field=field, old_value=sorted(o), new_value=sorted(n), change_type="modified"))
    return changes
```
and at the call site:
```python
            elif baseline_action and current_action:
                changes = self._compare_actions(baseline_action, current_action)
                status = "modified" if changes else "unchanged"
                diffs.append(ActionDiff(key=key, status=status, changes=changes))
```
`_write_action_changes` (`differ.py:216-235`) currently renders only added and
removed; extend it to render modified, mirroring `_write_workflow_changes`.
Add a test passing two genuinely different manifests under one key.

## Resolution
Implemented Differ._compare_actions over name/description/author/runs/is_composite/is_docker/is_javascript plus inputs/outputs, and extended _write_action_changes to render a Modified Actions section. 3 new differ tests passing two genuinely different manifests under one key.
title: diff_actions marks every pre-existing action unchanged, so version drift is never detected

body:
## Problem

`AuditServiceFactory.create` constructs a `Cache` (sqlite-backed) and a
`GitHubClient` (httpx connection pool). Both expose `close()`, and
`GitHubClient` implements the context-manager protocol. Nothing in the
production code path ever calls either.

## Evidence

`factory.py:49` — `cache = Cache(cache_dir)`
`factory.py:54` — `client = GitHubClient(token)`

Neither object is stored anywhere that closes it: `AuditService.__init__`
(`services.py:41-54`) keeps only `scanner`, `parser`, `analyzer`, `resolver`,
`validator`. `Resolver` (`resolver.py:20-32`) holds `github_client` and `cache`
as plain attributes with no `__del__`, no `close`, and no context manager.
`cli.py` never closes anything.

Exhaustive scan for call sites:
```
$ grep -rn '\.close()\|__enter__\|with .*GitHubClient\|with .*Cache' ghaw_auditor/ tests/
ghaw_auditor/cache.py:47:        self.cache.close()          <- definition
ghaw_auditor/github_client.py:120:  self.client.close()       <- definition
ghaw_auditor/github_client.py:122:  def __enter__(...)        <- definition
tests/test_cache.py:12,23,36,58                               <- tests only
tests/test_github_client.py:20,30,39,137,152                  <- tests only
```
Every call site is a test. Production code has none.

Observable today: the test run emits five
`ResourceWarning: unclosed database in <sqlite3.Connection object ...>` from
`_pytest/unraisableexception.py` — the leak surfacing through the paths that
*do* exercise the factory.

Failing scenario: `diskcache.Cache` holds an open sqlite connection and file
handle per instance. A long-lived process that calls
`AuditServiceFactory.create` per repository — the natural way to use this as a
library across an org's repos — accumulates one sqlite connection and one httpx
pool per call until it hits the process file-descriptor limit and every
subsequent open fails.

## Impact

For a single short CLI invocation, interpreter shutdown papers over it. For the
library use the factory exists to enable, it is an unbounded descriptor leak.
Unflushed diskcache writes at abrupt termination also risk losing cache entries
that were paid for with real API calls.

## Fix

Give `AuditService` deterministic ownership of what the factory opened:

```python
class AuditService:
    def __init__(
        self, scanner, parser, analyzer, resolver=None, validator=None, _closeables: list[Any] | None = None
    ) -> None:
        ...
        self._closeables = _closeables or []

    def close(self) -> None:
        for c in self._closeables:
            try:
                c.close()
            except Exception:  # never mask the real result
                logger.debug("close failed", exc_info=True)

    def __enter__(self) -> AuditService:
        return self

    def __exit__(self, *exc: Any) -> None:
        self.close()
```
Factory passes `_closeables=[cache] + ([client] if client else [])`; `cli.py`
uses `with AuditServiceFactory.create(...) as service:`. This also removes the
ResourceWarnings from the test output.

## Resolution
AuditService now takes closeables, implements close()/__enter__/__exit__; factory passes [cache] + [client]; cli.scan uses 'with'. Proven directly: with the context manager 0 ResourceWarnings, without closing 1. A failing close is logged, never masks the audit result. 2 new factory tests. Residual warnings in the suite originate in unittest.mock internals, not the production path.
title: Cache and GitHubClient are never closed: sqlite connection and HTTP pool leak every run

body:
## Problem

`_resolve_github_action` writes each fetched manifest to a
`NamedTemporaryFile(delete=False)` and unlinks it after parsing. The unlink is
not protected: if parsing raises, the `except` block returns and the temp file
is never removed.

## Evidence

`resolver.py:150-164`:
```python
try:
    import tempfile

    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", suffix=".yml", delete=False) as f:
        f.write(manifest_content)
        temp_path = Path(f.name)

    manifest = self.parser.parse_action(temp_path)  # <-- may raise
    temp_path.unlink()  # <-- skipped if it does
    return action.canonical_key(), manifest
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Failed to parse manifest for {action.canonical_key()}: {e}")
    return "", None
```
`parse_action` raises on malformed YAML (ruamel scanner errors) and explicitly
raises `ValueError(f"Empty action file: {path}")` at `parser.py:329-330`. Both
land in the `except` with the file still on disk.

Failing scenario: scan a repo referencing an action whose upstream `action.yml`
is empty or malformed. Each scan run leaves one orphaned
`/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX.yml`. Nothing ever reaps them — `delete=False` opts out of
the OS-level cleanup that `NamedTemporaryFile` normally provides. A scheduled
audit across many repos accumulates these until `/tmp` fills.

The leak is concurrent: `resolve_actions` (`resolver.py:38`) runs this under a
`ThreadPoolExecutor`, so a repo with many broken references leaks several files
per run in parallel.

Secondary defect at the same site: `import tempfile` at `resolver.py:152` is a
function-local import inside a hot loop. Every other module imports at the top;
`ruff` does not flag it because it is syntactically legal.

## Impact

Unbounded disk growth in `/tmp` on any host running repeated scans, triggered by
input the tool does not control (a third party's malformed manifest). On a
shared CI runner or a long-lived audit host this eventually fails unrelated
processes.

## Fix

The file only exists because `parse_action` takes a path. Guarantee cleanup with
`try/finally`, and hoist the import:

```python
temp_path: Path | None = None
try:
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(mode="w", suffix=".yml", delete=False, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write(manifest_content)
        temp_path = Path(f.name)
    manifest = self.parser.parse_action(temp_path)
    return action.canonical_key(), manifest
except Exception as e:
    logger.error(f"Failed to parse manifest for {action.canonical_key()}: {e}")
    return "", None
finally:
    if temp_path is not None:
        temp_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
```
Move `import tempfile` to the module header alongside the other stdlib imports.

Better still, remove the temp file entirely by giving `Parser` a
`parse_action_content(content: str, origin: str)` that loads from a string —
`parse_action` becomes a thin wrapper that reads the file and delegates. That
deletes the whole failure mode rather than cleaning up after it.

## Resolution
Removed the temp file entirely rather than guarding it: added Parser.parse_action_content(content, origin, default_name) and resolver now parses fetched manifests from memory. parse_action is a thin wrapper. The failure mode no longer exists; the function-local 'import tempfile' is gone with it.
title: Temp file leaks on every remote manifest that fails to parse

body:
## Problem

`Policy.min_permissions` defaults to `True` and is documented as the
least-privilege control, but `PolicyValidator` never branches on it. Enabling it
does nothing. `Policy.custom_rules` is likewise never read.

## Evidence

```
$ grep -rn 'min_permissions' ghaw_auditor/ tests/ README.md
ghaw_auditor/models.py:195:    min_permissions: bool = True
README.md:222:min_permissions: true             # Enforce least-privilege
```
Two hits: the declaration and the documentation. No read anywhere.

The validator branches on exactly three fields:
```
$ sed -n '/def _validate_workflow/,/return violations/p' ghaw_auditor/policy.py | grep 'self.policy'
        if self.policy.require_pinned_actions:
        if self.policy.forbid_branch_refs:
        if self.policy.require_concurrency_on_pr:
```
`min_permissions` and `custom_rules` (`models.py:195,201`) are absent.

`README.md:205-233` presents `min_permissions: true` inside the copy-paste
`policy.yml` template and lists it under "Enforce least-privilege".

This is the same defect class as the ignored `--policy` file, and it becomes
*more* dangerous once that loader is fixed: previously every policy field was
inert, so nothing stood out. Now that the other four fields genuinely take
effect, a user reasonably concludes the whole file is honoured — and
`min_permissions` is the one that silently is not.

Failing scenario: a user writes `min_permissions: true`, runs
`ghaw-auditor validate --policy policy.yml --enforce` against a workflow that
declares `permissions: write-all`, and gets "No policy violations found".

## Impact

A documented security control that is a no-op. Least-privilege on the job token
is the highest-value check this tool could offer — it is the mitigation for the
`write-all` exposure — and it is advertised, defaulted on, and absent.

## Fix

Implement the check, gated on the flag, in `_validate_workflow`:

```python
        if self.policy.min_permissions:
            violations.extend(self._check_min_permissions(workflow_path, workflow))
```
with two rules that are unambiguous and cheap:

- **write-all** — every scope set to WRITE is maximally permissive: `error`.
- **no permissions declared anywhere** (neither workflow nor any job) — the job
  token silently inherits the repository default, which for many repos is
  read/write on contents: `warning`.

Both are now detectable because `_parse_permissions` expands the bare-string
forms rather than discarding them.

Separately, either implement `custom_rules` or remove it from `models.py:201`;
an unread list of rule objects is dead public surface.

## Resolution
Implemented _check_min_permissions: write-all at workflow or job level is an error, nothing declared anywhere is a warning. Gated on the flag. Removed Policy.custom_rules and the PolicyRule model (breaking, recorded in CHANGELOG) rather than leave a second unread field. 5 new policy tests. README rules list updated.
title: Policy.min_permissions is documented as enforcing least-privilege but is never read

body:
## Problem

The `yamllint` pre-commit hook exits 1 against files already committed to the
repository. Since `default_install_hook_types: [pre-commit, commit-msg]` is set,
every `git commit` in this repo fails until the author bypasses the hooks
entirely.

## Evidence

```
$ pre-commit run yamllint --all-files >/dev/null 2>&1; echo $?
1
```
The failures are on committed, unmodified content — verified against `HEAD`, not
the working tree:
```
$ git show HEAD:.github/workflows/pr.yml | awk 'length>80 {print NR": "length" chars"}'
15: 82 chars
36: 82 chars
47: 87 chars
```
Those are the SHA-pinned action lines, e.g.
`      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c771a70e6277c0a99b617c7a806ffedaca235ff9 # v9.0.0`
A 40-char SHA pin plus the conventional `# vX.Y.Z` comment cannot fit in 80
columns. The repo's own security practice (SHA pinning) is incompatible with its
linter's default line limit.

Also reported on every workflow and fixture:
- `4:1 warning truthy value should be one of [false, true] (truthy)` — this is
  the GitHub Actions `on:` key, which YAML 1.1 reads as the boolean `on`. It is
  unavoidable in any Actions workflow.
- `too few spaces before comment` on each SHA pin.

**Root cause: yamllint has no configuration and is running on defaults.**
```
$ ls -a | grep -i yamllint
.yamlignore
$ cat .yamlignore
# Ignore patterns for yamllint
```
`.yamlignore` is not a file yamllint reads. yamllint looks for `.yamllint`,
`.yamllint.yaml`, or `.yamllint.yml`; none exists. So the file is dead config
that reads as though exclusions are configured when none are in effect, and
yamllint applies its stock 80-column rule.

## Impact

A failing pre-commit gate trains contributors to run `git commit --no-verify`,
which disables *every* hook in the file — including `gitleaks` (secret
detection), `detect-private-key`, `actionlint`, `checkov`, and `ruff`. One
misconfigured cosmetic linter therefore disables the repository's entire
security tooling in practice. The blast radius is far larger than the cosmetic
complaint that causes it.

## Fix

Add a real yamllint config at the repo root so the linter matches the project's
actual conventions:

```yaml
# .yamllint.yaml
extends: default

rules:
  # SHA-pinned actions plus their `# vX.Y.Z` comment exceed 80 columns.
  # 120 matches [tool.ruff] line-length in pyproject.toml.
  line-length:
    max: 120
  # `on:` is a GitHub Actions key, not a truthy scalar. Unavoidable in workflows.
  truthy:
    check-keys: false
  # `@<sha> # v1.2.3` is the conventional single-space pin annotation.
  comments:
    min-spaces-from-content: 1
```
Then delete `.yamlignore`, or rename its content into the `ignore:` key of the
new config where it will actually take effect.

## Resolution
Added .yamllint.yaml (line-length 120 to match ruff, truthy check-keys false for the Actions 'on:' key, comments min-spaces-from-content 1 for SHA pins) and deleted the dead .yamlignore. yamllint now Passes; the full pre-commit suite is green, so commits no longer require --no-verify. Also added .markdownlint-cli2.yaml with MD024 siblings_only, without which the next Keep-a-Changelog release entry would block commits the same way.
title: yamllint fails on the repo's own committed files, blocking every commit; .yamlignore is dead config

## Problem

Action allow/deny patterns are turned into regexes by replacing `*` with `.*`
and interpolating the rest raw. Every other regex metacharacter in the pattern
keeps its regex meaning, and an unbalanced one raises `re.error`.

## Evidence

`policy.py:160-163`:
```python
    def _matches_pattern(self, action_id: str, pattern: str) -> bool:
        regex_pattern = pattern.replace("*", ".*")
        return bool(re.match(f"^{regex_pattern}$", action_id))
```
Two distinct failures:

1. **Silent over-match.** `.` is the common case, since org and repo names
   legitimately contain dots. A deny pattern `evil.org/tool` compiles to
   `^evil.org/tool$`, where `.` matches any character — so `evilXorg/tool` is
   also denied, and an allow pattern is correspondingly too permissive. An
   allowlist that matches more than it should is a security failure: it admits
   actions the author never approved.

2. **Crash on metacharacters.** A pattern containing `[`, `(`, `+` or `?` in an
   unbalanced position raises `re.error`. `_matches_pattern` is called from
   `_check_action_allowlist` (`policy.py:115,127`), which is called from
   `validate`, which `cli.py` runs inside the blanket `except Exception`
   (`cli.py:171`) — so a typo in a user's policy file surfaces as
   `Scan failed: ...` with exit code 2, indistinguishable from a tool crash.
   `validate` (`cli.py:209-260`) has no handler at all, so there it is an
   uncaught traceback.

This becomes reachable input the moment the `--policy` loading defect is fixed
(filed separately) — today `denied_actions`/`allowed_actions` are always empty
because the policy file is ignored, which is the only reason this has not been
hit.

## Impact

An allowlist that over-matches silently admits unapproved actions, defeating the
control. A malformed pattern turns a policy typo into an opaque crash rather
than a clear validation error.

## Fix

Escape the literal parts and translate only the wildcard. `fnmatch` already
implements exactly this and is stdlib:

```python
from fnmatch import fnmatchcase


def _matches_pattern(self, action_id: str, pattern: str) -> bool:
    return fnmatchcase(action_id, pattern)
```
`fnmatchcase` gives `*`, `?` and `[seq]` glob semantics, treats every other
character literally, and cannot raise on user input. It is also what users
expect from a pattern that documents `*` as its wildcard.

## Resolution
Replaced the hand-built regex with fnmatchcase. A dot is now literal (verified: deny 'evil.org/tool' no longer matches 'evilXorg/tool') and a malformed pattern like 'a/[b' no longer raises. 2 new policy tests.
title: _matches_pattern builds a regex from policy strings without escaping: over-match and crash

body:
## Problem

`Analyzer.analyze_workflows` takes `actions: dict[str, ActionManifest]` and
never references it. Callers resolve every action over the network to build that
dict, then hand it to a function that discards it.

## Evidence

`analyzer.py:20-34` — the parameter appears in the signature and nowhere in the
body:
```
$ sed -n '20,35p' ghaw_auditor/analyzer.py | grep -n 'actions'
2:        self, workflows: dict[str, WorkflowMeta], actions: dict[str, ActionManifest]
```
One hit, the signature line. The returned `analysis` dict is built entirely from
`workflows`; none of `_analyze_triggers`, `_analyze_permissions`,
`_analyze_secrets`, `_analyze_runners`, `_analyze_containers` takes an `actions`
argument.

Call site `services.py:84`:
```python
        analysis = self.analyzer.analyze_workflows(workflows, actions)
```
where `actions` is the result of `self.resolver.resolve_actions(...)`
(`services.py:81`) — one GitHub API round trip per unique action, plus manifest
fetches.

## Impact

Two costs. The dead parameter misleads every reader into believing the analysis
covers resolved manifests, when it is purely workflow-side; the report's
"Analysis" section (`renderer.py:91-119`) is therefore narrower than it appears.
And it advertises a natural extension point that was never built — action-level
statistics (composite vs docker vs javascript counts, actions missing
descriptions, unpinned-by-manifest) are the obvious content for an "Analysis"
section and are exactly what this argument was reserved for.

## Fix

Either use it or drop it. Using it is the better outcome since the data is
already paid for:

```python
    def _analyze_actions(self, actions: dict[str, ActionManifest]) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {
            "total_resolved": len(actions),
            "composite": sum(1 for a in actions.values() if a.is_composite),
            "docker": sum(1 for a in actions.values() if a.is_docker),
            "javascript": sum(1 for a in actions.values() if a.is_javascript),
            "missing_description": sorted(k for k, a in actions.items() if not a.description),
        }
```
and add `"actions": self._analyze_actions(actions)` to the returned dict, with a
matching section in `renderer._write_analysis`.

If action analysis is genuinely not wanted, delete the parameter and update the
single call site — but do not leave a resolved-and-discarded network result in
the hot path.

## Resolution
Implemented Analyzer._analyze_actions (total_resolved, composite, docker, javascript, missing_description) and added it to the analysis dict; Renderer._write_actions_analysis renders it. The resolved manifests the resolver pays network cost for are now used instead of discarded. deduplicate_actions also retyped from list[Any]/dict[str,Any] to ActionRef.
title: analyze_workflows accepts an actions argument it never uses

body:
## Problem

`_handle_diff_mode` catches `FileNotFoundError`, logs it, and returns normally.
`scan` then prints its success banner and exits 0. A diff that never ran is
indistinguishable from a diff that found no changes.

## Evidence

`cli.py:61-78`:
```python
def _handle_diff_mode(result, baseline, output) -> None:
    console.print("[cyan]Running diff...[/cyan]")
    diff_service = DiffService(Differ(baseline))
    try:
        workflow_diffs, action_diffs = diff_service.compare(...)
        ...
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
        logger.error(f"Baseline not found: {e}")
        # falls through, returns None
```
`Differ.load_baseline` raises exactly this at `differ.py:37-38` when
`actions.json` or `workflows.json` is absent.

Control then returns to `cli.py:158`, continues to line 165
(`console.print("[green]✓ Audit complete! Reports in {output}[/green]")`) and
the command exits 0.

Failing scenario: CI runs `ghaw-auditor scan --diff --baseline .audit/baseline`
where a previous step failed to restore the cached baseline. The user sees
`✓ Audit complete!` and a zero exit. No `report.diff.md` is written, so a job
that greps it for changes finds nothing and concludes nothing changed. An
explicitly requested comparison silently did not happen.

Related ordering defect at the same site: `cli.py:165` prints the success banner
*before* `_enforce_policy` runs at `cli.py:168-169`, so an enforced failure
prints `✓ Audit complete!` immediately before failing.

## Impact

`--diff` is an explicit user request. Silently skipping it while reporting
success converts a setup error into a false "no changes detected" — the same
failure class as the ignored policy file: the tool reports safety it never
verified.

## Fix

A requested diff that cannot run is a failure:

```python
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        console.print(f"[red]Baseline not found: {e}[/red]")
        raise typer.Exit(1) from e
```
(This requires the `except typer.Exit: raise` passthrough from the exit-code
finding, or it will surface as exit 2.)

Separately, move the `✓ Audit complete!` print to after `_enforce_policy` so the
banner only appears on a genuinely clean run.

## Resolution
_handle_diff_mode now raises typer.Exit(1) on a missing baseline instead of logging and continuing. Verified: scan --diff with an absent baseline exits 1, was 0. The success banner was also moved after enforcement so it cannot precede a failure.
title: Diff mode fails open: a missing baseline logs an error but the run still reports success

body:
## Problem

`find_actions` walks the whole repository tree twice with `rglob`, with no
directory pruning. It descends into `.git`, `.venv`, `node_modules`, `build`,
and every vendored dependency.

## Evidence

`scanner.py:66-81`:
```python
        actions_dir = self.repo_path / ".github" / "actions"
        if actions_dir.exists():
            for action_file in actions_dir.rglob("action.y*ml"):        # pass 1
                ...
        for name in ("action.yml", "action.yaml"):
            for action_file in self.repo_path.rglob(name):              # pass 2, whole repo
                if ".github/workflows" in str(action_file.relative_to(self.repo_path)):
                    continue
                if not self._should_exclude(action_file) and action_file not in actions:
```
The only exclusion is `.github/workflows` and whatever the caller passed as
`exclude_patterns` — which no CLI caller ever passes (`cli.py:132-139` omits it),
so in practice the default is no exclusions at all.

Three separate costs:
1. **Traversal.** `rglob` on a repo with a populated `node_modules` or `.venv`
   walks hundreds of thousands of directory entries, twice.
2. **False positives.** A vendored dependency containing its own `action.yml`
   (common — many npm and Python packages vendor GitHub Actions) is reported as
   an action belonging to the audited repository.
3. **O(n^2) dedup.** `action_file not in actions` is a linear scan of a list
   inside the loop.

Pass 1 is also fully redundant: pass 2 covers `.github/actions` already, and the
`not in actions` check exists only to suppress the duplicates pass 1 created.

## Impact

On a large monorepo this dominates scan time before a single API call is made,
and it silently inflates the action inventory with third-party manifests the
repository does not own — corrupting the very inventory the tool exists to
produce.

## Fix

Prune during traversal and use a set for dedup:

```python
_SKIP_DIRS = {
    ".git",
    ".venv",
    "venv",
    "node_modules",
    "__pycache__",
    ".tox",
    ".mypy_cache",
    ".pytest_cache",
    "dist",
    "build",
}


def find_actions(self) -> list[Path]:
    actions: set[Path] = set()
    for dirpath, dirnames, filenames in os.walk(self.repo_path):
        dirnames[:] = [d for d in dirnames if d not in self._SKIP_DIRS]
        here = Path(dirpath)
        if here == self.repo_path / ".github" / "workflows":
            continue
        for name in ("action.yml", "action.yaml"):
            if name in filenames:
                p = here / name
                if not self._should_exclude(p):
                    actions.add(p)
    logger.info(f"Found {len(actions)} action files")
    return sorted(actions)
```
`os.walk` allows in-place pruning of `dirnames`, which `rglob` cannot do. This
also drops the redundant first pass and fixes the quadratic dedup.

Secondary defect at `scanner.py:77`: `".github/workflows" in str(rel_path)`
compares a forward-slash literal against a `str(Path)` that uses `\` on Windows,
so the workflows directory is not excluded there. The `os.walk` form above
compares Path objects and is separator-correct.

## Resolution
Replaced the double rglob with a single os.walk that prunes SKIP_DIRS in place (.git, .venv, node_modules, __pycache__, build, dist, ...), dedups via a set instead of an O(n^2) list scan, drops the redundant .github/actions pass, and compares Path objects rather than a forward-slash string so the workflows-dir exclusion is separator-correct.
title: find_actions rglobs the entire repo including .git, .venv and node_modules

## Problem

The pin detector matches only 40 lowercase hex characters, so a legitimately
pinned action written in uppercase, or pinned to a SHA-256 object id, is
reported as unpinned.

## Evidence

`policy.py:64`:
```python
if action.type == ActionType.GITHUB and action.ref and not re.match(r"^[a-f0-9]{40}$", action.ref):
```
- `[a-f0-9]` excludes `A-F`. Git accepts and many tools emit uppercase hex;
  `uses: actions/checkout@3D3C42E5AAC5BA805825DA76410C181273BA90B1` is a valid
  full pin and is flagged as a violation.
- `{40}` is SHA-1 only. Git's SHA-256 object format produces 64-character ids;
  a repository using it cannot pin in a way this check accepts.

The message compounds the confusion — it prints
`is not pinned to SHA: <the SHA>`, naming the very SHA it failed to recognise.

Also note `re.match(r"...$", ref)` on a ref containing a newline would match up
to the newline (`$` matches before a trailing `\n`); use `\Z` for a strict
end-of-string anchor.

## Impact

False positives on correctly-pinned workflows. With `--enforce`, a compliant
repository fails its own gate, and the fastest way for a user to make the error
go away is to stop pinning — the check actively discourages the practice it
exists to enforce.

## Fix

```python
_SHA_RE = re.compile(r"^(?:[a-fA-F0-9]{40}|[a-fA-F0-9]{64})\Z")
...
if action.type in _REMOTE_TYPES and action.ref and not _SHA_RE.match(action.ref):
```
Compile once at module level rather than per call.

## Resolution
SHA_RE now accepts 40- or 64-char hex in either case, anchored with \\Z, compiled once at module level. 1 new policy test covering an uppercase SHA-1 and a SHA-256 pin.
title: Pinned-SHA check rejects uppercase hex and does not recognise SHA-256 refs

body:
## Problem

Two input-shape defects in the parser: a missing `runs-on` is invented rather
than reported, and an explicitly-null `runs:` block raises `AttributeError`.

## Evidence

**1. Fabricated runner.** `parser.py:128`:
```python
        runs_on = data.get("runs-on", "ubuntu-latest" if not is_reusable_call else "")
```
A job with no `runs-on` is invalid in GitHub Actions — the workflow will not
run. The parser records `ubuntu-latest` as though it were declared. That value
flows into `analyzer._analyze_runners` (`analyzer.py:64-71`), which tallies
runner usage, and into `renderer._write_job_details` (`renderer.py:124`), which
prints `Runner: \`ubuntu-latest\``. An auditor asked "what runners does this org
use" gets a count containing runners nobody configured, and the actual defect —
an invalid workflow — is never surfaced.

**2. Crash on null `runs`.** `parser.py:357-360`:
```python
        runs = data.get("runs", {})
        is_composite = runs.get("using") == "composite"
        ...
        is_javascript = runs.get("using", "").startswith("node")
```
`data.get("runs", {})` returns the default only when the key is *absent*. An
action file containing
```yaml
runs:
```
parses `runs` as `None`, so `runs.get` raises
`AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'`.
The same shape breaks line 360 even when `runs` is a dict: `runs.get("using", "")`
returns `None` (not `""`) if `using:` is present but empty, and
`None.startswith` raises.

This is reachable from untrusted input — `_resolve_github_action`
(`resolver.py:158`) parses manifests fetched from arbitrary third-party
repositories. The exception is caught by the broad handler at `resolver.py:162`
and logged as "Failed to parse manifest", so a malformed upstream action is
misreported as a parse failure of unknown cause.

## Impact

Fabricated runner data corrupts the inventory that is the tool's primary output.
The null-`runs` crash turns a third party's malformed manifest into an
unexplained resolution failure.

## Fix

```python
        runs_on = data.get("runs-on")
        if runs_on is None:
            runs_on = ""
            if not is_reusable_call:
                logger.warning(f"Job '{name}' in {path} declares no runs-on")
```
and make the `runs` lookups null-safe:
```python
        runs = data.get("runs") or {}
        using = runs.get("using") or ""
        is_composite = using == "composite"
        is_docker = using in ("docker", "Dockerfile")
        is_javascript = using.startswith("node")
```
`JobMeta.runs_on` (`models.py:135`) is already `str | list[str]`, so `""`
validates. Consumers that count runners should skip empty values.

## Resolution
runs-on is no longer defaulted to ubuntu-latest: absent means '' plus a warning naming the job and file. The runs block uses 'data.get("runs") or {}' and 'runs.get("using") or ""' so a present-but-null key cannot raise AttributeError. Existing test updated from asserting the fabricated default; 1 new test for the null runs block.
title: Parser fabricates runs-on: ubuntu-latest for jobs that declare none, and crashes on a null runs block

body:
## Problem

The suite reports 100% line coverage and 211 passing tests, yet none of the
Critical/High defects in this audit are caught by it. Two specific patterns are
responsible.

## Evidence

**1. No exact-count assertions in policy tests.** Every positive assertion in
`test_policy.py` is a existence check:
```
$ grep -nE 'len\(violations\)' tests/test_policy.py
51:    assert len(violations) > 0
85:    assert len(violations) == 0
125:    assert len(violations) > 0
166:    assert len(violations) > 0
207:    assert len(violations) > 0
226:    assert len(violations) > 0
246:    assert len(violations) == 0
```
Five `> 0` and two `== 0`. The duplicate-violation defect emits exactly twice
the correct count; `> 0` is satisfied by both the correct and the broken
behaviour, so no test changes state when the bug is fixed or reintroduced.

**2. Policy-file tests assert nothing about the policy.**
`test_cli.py:111-127` writes a genuine policy file:
```python
    policy_file = tmp_path / "policy.yml"
    policy_file.write_text("require_pinned_actions: true")
```
passes `--policy-file`, and asserts only the exit code. Since `cli.py:128` never
reads the file, these tests pass while the feature is a documented no-op. They
would pass unchanged if `--policy-file` were deleted from the CLI — the
definition of a tautological test.

**3. Untested surfaces behind the coverage number.** Line coverage counts a line
as covered when it executes, not when its behaviour is asserted:
- `grep -rn 'REUSABLE\|reusable' tests/test_policy.py` -> no hits. The
  reusable-workflow policy blind spot has no test.
- `grep -rn 'write-all' tests/` -> only `test_parser.py:263-265`, which calls
  `_parse_permissions("read-all")` and asserts an object is returned, never that
  the level was captured. It locks in the discard.
- `test_differ.py:302-313` passes the *same object* as baseline and current and
  asserts `unchanged` — it cannot detect the missing comparison.
- No test asserts `exit_code == 1` for an enforced violation.

## Impact

`--cov-fail-under=70` with 100% actual coverage reads as a strong safety net and
is treated as one by `CONTRIBUTING.md:42`. In practice the suite pins the
current behaviour rather than the intended behaviour, so all five
Critical/High defects here shipped green. Fixing them will require *changing*
tests that currently pass, which is the signature of tests written against the
implementation instead of the contract.

## Fix

- Replace every `len(violations) > 0` in `test_policy.py` with the exact
  expected count.
- Make the policy-file tests assert an effect, not an exit code: write a policy
  that denies an action the fixture uses, and assert the violation appears.
- Add the missing cases named above: reusable workflow on `@main`, `write-all`
  expansion, two differing manifests under one key, `exit_code == 1` under
  `--enforce`.
- Consider `--cov-branch`; line coverage cannot see the untaken branches that
  hide several of these.

## Resolution
test_policy.py converted from 'len(violations) > 0' to exact counts and scoped per rule. Policy-file CLI tests now assert an effect (a denied action appears, a disabled rule suppresses) rather than an exit code, so they can no longer pass with the feature removed. Added the missing cases: reusable workflow on @main, write-all expansion, two differing manifests under one key, exit_code == 1 under --enforce. Suite 211 -> 244 tests and floor 70 -> 85 at the time this finding was resolved. Final shipped state, after the remaining audit fixes and the PR review round: 267 tests, branch coverage now measured (--cov-branch), floor raised to 100%, actual 100%.
title: Policy tests assert only len(violations) > 0, hiding the double-count; policy-file CLI tests are tautological

body:
## Problem

The documentation describes behaviour the code does not implement, and states a
coverage threshold that disagrees with the enforced one.

## Evidence

**1. `--policy` documented as working in seven places.** `README.md:40,133,237,240,334`
show `--policy policy.yml --enforce` as a working invocation, `README.md:138`
documents the flag, and `README.md:207` presents a full `policy.yml` schema for
users to copy. `CHANGELOG.md` lists "Policy validation with enforcement" under
the 1.0.0 Added section. The loader is a `# TODO` at `cli.py:128` and
`cli.py:242` — the file is never read (filed separately as Critical).
Documentation is not merely stale here; it actively instructs users to depend on
a silent no-op.

**2. Coverage floor contradiction.**
```
README.md:476        - Coverage >= 85%
CONTRIBUTING.md:42   - Maintain coverage >= 85%
pyproject.toml:59    addopts = "... --cov-fail-under=70"
```
The docs promise 85%; CI fails only below 70. Actual coverage is 100%, so the
gap is latent — but a contributor who drops coverage to 72% satisfies the gate
while violating the stated standard, and no reviewer signal fires.

**3. `--exclude` has no CLI flag.** `AuditServiceFactory.create` accepts
`exclude_patterns` (`factory.py:29`) and `Scanner` implements it
(`scanner.py:31-34`), but `cli.py:132-139` never passes it and no CLI option
declares it. The capability is unreachable for any user of the published
command.

## Impact

The `--policy` documentation is the harmful one: it converts a missing feature
into a false security assurance, because a user following the README will
believe an enforced policy gate is in place. The coverage mismatch and the
unreachable exclude are ordinary drift.

## Fix

- After the `--policy` loader is implemented, the docs become accurate; until
  then they must not claim it works.
- Align the thresholds: set `--cov-fail-under=85` in `pyproject.toml:59` to match
  the documented standard (current coverage is 100%, so this is free), or lower
  the docs to 70. Matching the docs is the better direction.
- Either expose `--exclude` as a repeatable CLI option threaded through to
  `AuditServiceFactory.create(exclude_patterns=...)`, or remove the parameter.

## Resolution
--policy docs became accurate when the loader landed. Coverage floor raised to 85% in pyproject to match README/CONTRIBUTING (actual 100%). --exclude exposed as a repeatable CLI option and documented. Added an exit-code table and corrected the flag name to --policy-file. Policy rules list now documents min_permissions and states that all rules apply to reusable workflow calls.
title: README documents a non-functional --policy feature and a coverage floor the config does not enforce

body:
## Problem

The project declares itself MIT-licensed in package metadata and documentation
but ships no license text.

## Evidence

```
$ ls LICENSE* COPYING* NOTICE*
  *** NO LICENSE FILE ***
```
`pyproject.toml:7` — `license = {text = "MIT"}`
`README.md:464` — a `## License` heading
`git ls-files` confirms no license file is tracked anywhere in the repo.

The package is publishable: `[project.scripts]` (`pyproject.toml:30-31`) defines
the `ghaw-auditor` entry point and `[build-system]` uses hatchling, so a wheel
built today asserts MIT in its metadata while carrying no license text and no
copyright line.

## Impact

`license = {text = "MIT"}` states the license but supplies neither the full
terms nor the copyright attribution the MIT license itself requires ("The above
copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all copies").
Downstream consumers running license-compliance tooling get a bare SPDX string
with no verifiable text; some scanners classify this as unlicensed. For a
security-auditing tool intended for enterprise CI, an unresolvable license is a
practical adoption blocker.

## Fix

Add a top-level `LICENSE` file with the standard MIT text and the copyright
line `Copyright (c) 2025 Ismo Vuorinen`, then modernise the declaration to the
PEP 639 form so the file is included in built distributions:

```toml
license = "MIT"
license-files = ["LICENSE"]
```
(hatchling supports both; the PEP 639 form is what current tooling reads.)

## Resolution
Added LICENSE with the full MIT text and 'Copyright (c) 2025 Ismo Vuorinen'. pyproject modernised to the PEP 639 form: license = "MIT" plus license-files = ["LICENSE"], so the text ships in built distributions.
title: No LICENSE file despite pyproject declaring MIT and README carrying a License section
